A sea urchin sperm swims a helix about 8.4 µm in radius, one winding each 0.38 s, at about 200 µm/s, its own winding bringing it a stimulus of about twice a second; while the baseline rises its helix bends smoothly toward the gradient, and while the baseline declines it makes a sharp turn, 31 such events in 9 of 10 cells. A dung beetle keeps a straight line away from the dung pile by sun, moon, the light's polarizing around them, and at night by the Milky Way's glow alone, and under overcast it loses its straight paths. A hunting dragonfly catches its prey about 95 times in 100, in under half a second, its head turning ahead of any drift to make up for it, its body turning to follow the angles between head and body. Most monarchs live about a month through four or five generations a year, and a super generation lives about eight times as long, flying up to about 3,000 miles, 50 to 100 miles a day, to oyamel firs in Mexico's Sierra Madre, none of them finishing the return, their offspring continuing it. On a tether in a magnetic field monarchs fly south, and with the field's inclination reversing they fly north; with light above 420 nm they circle, and with light above 380 nm they fly directionally. Coasts and the Rocky and Appalachian mountains are a field's proposal for guiding monarchs back when wind blows them off course.
